question: How's that going to affect the little guy?
answer: Well, you're seeing it right now. Because we have to remember while this is going on, say 2001, 2002, 2003, everybody was treating real estate and houses. It reminded me quite a bit of the tech drive of the late '90s that of course flopped eventually. This was everybody wanted into the pool and so these subprime lenders - eventually, the pool of very qualified applicants ran out, so what they did was they lowered their standards. And so you no longer needed to prove your income, you no longer had to have a credit history of 700, and they would still give you a loan. Admittedly, and then all these adjustable rate mortgages that eventually are going to balloon up in payments. But what we're seeing right now is all these people going in the bankruptcy, all these lenders going to bankruptcy, these loans being defaulted on. Now all of a sudden you try and get a loan, you know what, you better have your pay stubs, you better have your W-2s, you better have your credit history tight because they're not going to make these types of loans anymore. And of course who's going to suffer - well, I don't know if anyone's really going to suffer. Because if it means that you can't get a house that you can't really afford, I think that's a good thing.

question: And the city wants to depend on state funds and bonds that will be up for sale. This is part of rebuilding the territory of New Orleans, but how successful, Bob, is this going to be if there's not a federal buy in?
answer: Well, first of all, I have to say good for New Orleans. Stop waiting. Take it to yourself. Do your own thing because if the federal government proved anything during the aftermath of Katrina, you may not really want to be relying on them to come bail you out. Can it be successful without New Orleans? Sure. But I think they actually will need federal government help to get this money, because I don't know if just selling bonds is going to do it. But I do actually applaud New Orleans for actually taking this positive proactive step instead of just sitting back and waiting and complaining that the government's not here to help me.

question: Should these hospitals have more of a compunction to be full-service because they are essentially benefiting from doing these specialty operations? Bob, do they need to have more backup?
answer: Well, they're a boutique, right? Not only are they specialized but they also take the most expensive procedures and keep them for themselves. You would think that if you're going to a hospital and you get sick that there would be someone there to take care of you. That needs to be spelled out to the patient beforehand that, you know what, you're going to come here and you may not - if anything else goes wrong other than what we're here to treat you for, you may not come out of this all right. We may have to call 911. I don't know if I necessarily need the boutiques to change because, you know, you go and get your oil changed, you're not getting your hair done. So you know where you're going when you go to this place. You have to be aware of it, though. But it just sounds so bad for a hospital to call 911. That just sounds so bad. It seems like a situation that you would never ever want to happen and that you would need the doctors on call to be there immediately if something goes wrong. I don't know, but it just does not sound good.
